title: Feelings & opinions
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: perché is ONE word doing BOTH jobs: it asks "why" (Perché non mangi?) and it answers "because" (Non mangio perché non ho fame). Spanish separates the two in spelling and Italian does not, so there is no orthographic escape — the sentence around it is what tells you which one you are looking at.

quindi is the other direction: perché puts the REASON second, quindi puts the CONSEQUENCE second. The same two facts either way round — Non voglio il caffè perché sono stanco · Sono stanco, quindi non voglio il caffè.

A closed set of states runs on avere plus a BARE noun where English uses "be" plus an adjective: ho fame (I'm hungry) · ho freddo (I'm cold) · ho sete (I'm thirsty) · ho sonno (I'm sleepy) · ho caldo (I'm hot). No article, and never essere: sono fame is the classic English sentence and it says nothing.

Feelings that ARE adjectives take essere and agree with the SUBJECT — with whoever the sentence is about: sono stanco (a man about himself) · sono stanca (a woman) · sei felice? (asked of anyone, since felice has one shape). It is M2's agreement rule at a length where it finally has room to move.
The weather takes fare: fa caldo, fa freddo. The same noun that rides avere for a person rides fare for the day — ho freddo is about me, fa freddo is about the weather.
An opinion at this level is penso di plus a plain verb: penso di andare a Roma. penso che pulls in a mood Italian keeps for exactly this job (penso che sia…), and that belongs to a later level.

words.note: hunger — a noun, not an adjective, which is why the verb in front of it is avere and not essere. It stands bare, with no article: ho fame, never ho la fame.

sentences.trap: English makes hunger a state you ARE. Italian makes it a thing you HAVE. Sono fame is the sentence an English speaker writes first, and it means nothing at all.
sentences.sound: FA-me, two syllables with the final -e pronounced. It is one letter from fame in English and nothing like it in sound.

variations.cue: I'm not hungry
variations.changed: non in front of the verb — the noun behind it is untouched

variations.cue: Are you hungry?
variations.changed: ho → hai: the same state, asked

variations.cue: Anna is hungry
variations.changed: ho → ha for a third person; fame never moves

mistake.why: fame is a noun, so it takes avere: Ho fame. Sono fame would be claiming to BE hunger.

sentences.usage: The shortest complete sentence in the module, and the most used.
sentences.mnemonic: In Italian you HAVE hunger; in English you ARE hungry.

words.note: cold — a noun here, riding avere like fame: ho freddo. The same word does duty as an adjective elsewhere (un caffè freddo), and the verb in front of it is what tells you which job it is doing.

sentences.trap: The English word is an adjective and the Italian one is doing a noun's work. Once ho fame is in place, ho freddo, ho sete and ho sonno all follow the same shape.
sentences.sound: FRED-do, with the double d genuinely held — a single one would be a different word.

variations.cue: I'm not cold
variations.changed: non in front of the verb

variations.cue: Are you cold?
variations.changed: ho → hai: asked instead of stated

variations.cue: It's cold today
variations.changed: the same noun with fare instead of avere — now it is the weather, not me

mistake.why: This is a sentence, and it says you are a cold person. The state is ho freddo.

sentences.usage: Complaining, and asking for a window to be shut.
sentences.mnemonic: ho freddo is me; fa freddo is the day.

sentences.display: Non mangio perché non ho fame
sentences.cue: I'm not eating because I'm not hungry
sentences.glossEn: lit. "Not I-eat because not I-have hunger"
sentences.literal: Not I-eat because not I-have hunger

words.note: ONE word for both jobs. In the middle of a sentence it means "because" and introduces the reason; at the front of a question it means "why". Nothing about the spelling changes, and the accent on the final e is never optional.

sentences.trap: English uses two different words — why and because — and Spanish uses two different spellings. Italian uses one word for both, so the only clue is where it stands in the sentence.
sentences.sound: per-KE. The final é carries the stress and is a close e; the ch of that syllable is written che and said KE.

variations.cue: I'm not eating because I'm tired
variations.changed: swap the reason — perché takes any whole sentence behind it

variations.cue: Why aren't you eating?
variations.changed: the same word at the FRONT, where it asks instead of answering

variations.display: Non ho fame, quindi non mangio
variations.cue: I'm not hungry, so I'm not eating
variations.changed: the same two facts the other way round, joined by quindi

mistake.display: Non mangio perche non ho fame
mistake.why: perché carries an accent on its last letter, always. Without it, it is not a word.

sentences.mnemonic: One word, two directions: it asks at the front and answers in the middle.

sentences.display: Ho sete, quindi bevo un caffè
sentences.cue: I'm thirsty, so I'm having a coffee
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I-have thirst, so I-drink a coffee"
sentences.literal: I-have thirst, so I-drink a coffee

words.note: thirst, and another bare noun on avere: ho sete. Note the single t — sette with two is "seven", and Italian holds a doubled consonant long enough that the two are never confused out loud.
so — it introduces the CONSEQUENCE, where perché introduces the reason. It sits after a comma and takes a whole sentence behind it. così does the same job.

sentences.trap: perché and quindi are the same two facts in opposite orders. Choosing wrongly does not make a wrong sentence — it makes a sentence that says the opposite of what you meant.
sentences.sound: SE-te, with a single t, against alle sette with a doubled one. KWIN-di has the usual "kw" for qu.

variations.display: Bevo un caffè perché ho sete
variations.cue: I'm having a coffee because I'm thirsty
variations.changed: the same two facts with the reason second — perché instead of quindi

variations.display: Ho sete, quindi bevo un po' di acqua
variations.cue: I'm thirsty, so I'm drinking a bit of water
variations.changed: swap the consequence; quindi does not move

variations.cue: I'm not thirsty
variations.changed: the state on its own, negated

mistake.display: Ho sete, perché bevo un caffè
mistake.why: That says you are thirsty because you are drinking a coffee. The consequence takes quindi: Ho sete, quindi bevo un caffè.

sentences.usage: Explaining a decision in the same breath as making it.
sentences.mnemonic: perché looks back at the reason; quindi looks forward to what follows.

words.note: happy — a real adjective, so it takes essere and not avere. It ends in -e, so it has ONE shape for a man and a woman alike, and only goes plural: felici.

sentences.trap: The module's two halves sit side by side here: ho fame is a noun on avere, sono felice is an adjective on essere. Which verb you need depends on the WORD, not on the feeling.
sentences.sound: fe-LI-che. The c before e is soft — the ch of "church" — and the final -e is pronounced.

variations.cue: Are you happy?
variations.changed: sono → sei; felice has one shape, so nothing else moves

variations.display: Sono felice perché domani vado a Roma
variations.cue: I'm happy because tomorrow I'm going to Rome
variations.changed: a reason hung on with perché

variations.cue: I'm not happy today
variations.changed: non in front of the verb

mistake.why: felice is an adjective, so it takes essere: Sono felice oggi. avere is for the bare nouns — fame, freddo, sete.

sentences.usage: Saying how you are when "bene" is not enough.
sentences.mnemonic: A noun rides avere; an adjective rides essere.

words.note: sad — another -e adjective, so one shape for both genders and tristi in the plural. It rides essere, like felice.

sentences.trap: At the front of a question perché is "why", and the answer to it will use the very same word for "because". Nothing is added to ask — no "do", no inversion.
sentences.sound: TRI-ste, with a tapped r and a plain s before the t.

variations.cue: Why are you happy?
variations.changed: swap the adjective — the question word is the frame

variations.display: Sono triste perché non vedo Anna
variations.cue: I'm sad because I'm not seeing Anna
variations.changed: the answer, with the same word now meaning "because"

variations.cue: Why aren't you eating?
variations.changed: another verb behind the same question word, negated

mistake.why: Drop the tu — sei already says who is being asked. A pronoun here reads as an accusation.

sentences.usage: Asking after someone, once bene is clearly not the answer.
sentences.mnemonic: perché at the front is a question; perché in the middle is an answer.

sentences.cue: I'm thinking of going to Rome

words.note: "I'm thinking of" — and the di is compulsory in front of the plain verb that follows: penso di andare, penso di comprare. Taught whole, because penso on its own leads into penso che, which needs a mood this level does not teach.

sentences.trap: English says "I'm thinking of going" and "I think that I'll go" almost interchangeably. Italian's second one — penso che — needs a whole extra verb form, so this course stays on penso di and the plain verb.
sentences.sound: PEN-so. The s here is a plain s, not the z of casa: it follows a consonant rather than sitting between two vowels.

variations.cue: I'm thinking of buying a present
variations.changed: swap the plan — di stays in front of the plain verb

variations.display: Non penso di andare a Roma
variations.cue: I'm not thinking of going to Rome
variations.changed: non in front of the verb, and the rest is untouched

variations.display: Penso di andare a Roma perché ho una settimana libera
variations.cue: I'm thinking of going to Rome because I have a free week
variations.changed: a reason hung on with perché, at the length the module allows

mistake.why: The di is not optional after penso: Penso di andare a Roma.

sentences.usage: Floating a plan you have not committed to.
sentences.mnemonic: penso di + a plain verb; penso che is for a level that has the mood for it.

sentences.display: Ho sonno, quindi vado a casa
sentences.cue: I'm sleepy, so I'm going home
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I-have sleep, so I-go to home"
sentences.literal: I-have sleep, so I-go to home

words.note: The state of being sleepy — the fourth of the bare nouns on avere. Two n's: sono with one n is "I am", and the pair are a whole sentence apart.

sentences.trap: sonno and sono are one letter apart and the doubled n is held long enough that Italians never confuse them. On the page, the second n is what stands between "I'm sleepy" and "I am".
sentences.sound: SON-no, with the double n genuinely held — longer than the single n of sono.

variations.cue: I'm sleepy, so I'm not going out
variations.changed: swap the consequence; quindi is the hinge either way

variations.display: Vado a casa perché ho sonno
variations.cue: I'm going home because I'm sleepy
variations.changed: the same two facts reversed, so the joiner becomes perché

variations.cue: Are you sleepy?
variations.changed: ho → hai: the state, asked

mistake.display: Ho sono, quindi vado a casa
mistake.why: One n makes it "I have I-am". Sleepiness is sonno, with two.

sentences.mnemonic: Two n's for sleep, one n for being.

words.note: The same double life as freddo: a bare noun after avere (ho caldo — I'm hot) and after fare (fa caldo — it's hot out). As an adjective it agrees like any other: un caffè caldo, una pizza calda.

sentences.trap: English needs a subject — "it" — for the weather, and Italian refuses to write one. Fa caldo is the whole sentence, and fa is doing all the work.
sentences.sound: KAL-do. The l is clear and forward, and the a is open.

variations.cue: It's cold today
variations.changed: the other half of the weather, on the same verb

variations.cue: I'm hot
variations.changed: avere instead of fare — now it is me, not the day

variations.display: Fa caldo, quindi bevo un po' di acqua
variations.cue: It's hot, so I'm drinking a bit of water
variations.changed: a consequence hung on with quindi

mistake.why: About the weather it is fare, not essere: Fa caldo oggi. È caldo would be about a particular thing — il caffè è caldo.

sentences.usage: The most reliable small talk there is.
sentences.mnemonic: The day MAKES the weather: fa caldo, fa freddo.

sentences.cue: I don't want to go out because it's raining

words.note: "It rains" and "it is raining", in one word with no subject at all — Italian never writes an "it" for the weather. Its past is ha piovuto.

sentences.trap: One Italian word carries an English subject, a verb and a tense: piove is "it's raining". Adding anything in front of it — esso piove, lui piove — breaks the sentence.
sentences.sound: PYO-ve. The io is one syllable, and the v is soft and quick.

variations.cue: I'm not going out because it's raining
variations.changed: one verb instead of two — the reason is unchanged

variations.cue: It's raining, so I'm not going out
variations.changed: the same two facts the other way round, on quindi

variations.display: Non voglio uscire perché ho sonno
variations.cue: I don't want to go out because I'm sleepy
variations.changed: swap the reason — perché takes any whole sentence

mistake.display: Non voglio uscire perché esso piove
mistake.why: Nothing goes in front of piove. The weather has no subject in Italian: perché piove.

sentences.usage: The reason for staying in, in one clause.
sentences.mnemonic: piove is a whole English sentence in five letters.
